The Illusion of Abstract Man
The Critique:
Feuerbach preaches a "religion of love" and
an urge for happiness suited for all times and
peoples. But his abstract man does not live in
a historically determined world.
The Material Reality:
"Man thinks differently in a palace and in a
hut. If because of hunger, of misery, you have
no stuff in your body, you likewise have no
stuff for morality in your head."
The Stock Exchange Metaphor:
Under capitalist production, the Stock Exchange
becomes the highest temple of Feuerbach's
moral conduct -where the "urge to happiness"
is fulfilled so long as one speculates correctly,
masking a society split into classes.

The End of Classical Philosophy
The Expulsion:
Philosophy is expelled from nature
and history. It is no longer about
inventing interconnections in our
brains, but discovering them in
empirical facts. All that remains
is logic and dialectics.
The Betrayal:
Post-1848, the educated classes
of Germany abandoned theory
for stock-exchange speculation,
becoming undisguised
ideologists of the bourgeoisie.
The Inheritor:
Only the working-class
movement retains the fearles
zeal for theory. The more
ruthlessly disinterested
science proceeds, the more
it aligns with the aspirations
of the workers.
The German working-class movement is the inheritor of German classical philosophy.
